item.title: Causal Multiscale Modeling of Ocular FLASH Electroretinography: Model Development, Experimental Fitting, and Spin-Glass--Percolation Predictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.00103v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Purpose: To develop a causal multiscale model of retinal electroretinography (ERG) after ocular ultrahigh-dose-rate (FLASH) and conventional-dose-rate (CONV) irradiation, evaluate the framework against published ocular ERG data, and derive prospective dose-response predictions for future validation. Methods: The retina was coarse-grained into $N=200$ functional modules. Local rate equations were formulated as Hodgkin--Huxley-inspired conductance-balance/RC reductions of retinal ion-channel and synaptic pathways. Radiation generated an injury field that altered phototransduction, a-wave and b-wave dynamics and, in the network extension, inter-module coupling and bond survival. A reduced amplitude benchmark and nested M0/M1/M2 causal models were evaluated. Results: The reduced benchmark achieved $R^2=0.9721$ and RMSE $=11.94~\mu$V. M0, M1, and M2 yielded $R^2=0.8546$, 0.8559, and 0.8560, respectively, indicating limited independent identifiability of the network terms from amplitude data alone. Under an exploratory 50\% retained-gain criterion, the reduced benchmark predicted a-wave preservation thresholds of 28.6 Gy for FLASH and 23.7 Gy for CONV, and b-wave thresholds of 29.2 Gy and 24.1 Gy, respectively, corresponding to a model-based functional dose-modifying factor (DMF) of 1.21. Conclusion: The ERG amplitude data support the causal radiation-injury-to-ERG framework, while additional observables will be needed to distinguish the predicted collective-network contributions. The model also provides quantitative dose targets for prospective studies of the FLASH retinal-preservation window and a framework for testing how local retinal injury may propagate into collective dysfunction.
item.dc:creator: Ramin Abolfath, Mohammad Rezaee

item.title: Localized anomaly detection with a calorimeter normalizing flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.00234v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Normalizing flows trained as fast calorimeter simulators also give the likelihood of each shower, which can serve as an anomaly score. Because this likelihood sums over every voxel, a signal confined to a few voxels can be lost in the fluctuations of the rest of the shower. For example, in a public benchmark dataset in which a long-lived neutral particle decays to two photons, the CaloFlow likelihood used in previous work selects less than 5% of the signal at a background efficiency of $10^{-3}$ when the particle has the largest simulated mass and decays at or just behind the front face of the calorimeter. In this work, we define a regional anomaly score by summing the squared latent coordinates of the same flow within small detector regions around the point where the particle enters the calorimeter, with the threshold set using background showers alone. At the same background efficiency, this regional anomaly score selects more than 95% of the signal. The per-coordinate likelihood terms, summed over the same regions, perform equally well, but the squared latent coordinates have a known distribution for background showers and clearly illustrate when a shower departs from it. Therefore, normalizing flows may be sensitive to new physics, even if the global likelihood is not.
item.dc:creator: Raunav Mendiratta, Jason Weitz, Javier Duarte

item.title: Beyond Synthesis Conditions: Linking In-situ Growth Dynamics to Carbon Nanotube Forest Properties through Multimodal Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.00739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning for chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has largely mapped static synthesis conditions to final properties, implicitly treating these conditions as a complete description of growth. Here, we test this assumption by integrating gas-flow conditions with in-situ time-resolve growth profiles (growth curves) of vertically aligned CNT forests. We introduce an observation-window analysis, in which prediction is evaluated as a function of observation time by providing models with the growth curve only up to progressively later times, to determine not only whether a property can be predicted, but when the necessary information becomes available during synthesis. Clustering of normalized growth curves revealed distinct growth patterns independent of final forest height. The gas conditions alone could predict the initial growth rate but not the growth lifetime and failed to capture the variation in yield (R^2<0). Adding the growth curve improved yield prediction (R^2~0.4-0.5), with the relevant information emerging during the intermediate and later stages of growth rather than at its onset. In contrast, density and G/D ratio, which forest height does not record, showed no consistent improvement. The maximum height and lifetime could be estimated with moderate accuracy midway through the 10-min growth. Permutation feature importance identified water vapor and H_2, both linked to catalyst activity, as the most informative gas variables. These results indicate that variation unexplained by synthesis conditions is not merely noise but reflects an evolving catalyst state, and they establish mid-growth decision points for autonomous synthesis, enabling early termination of unpromising batches and, ultimately, in-batch adjustment of growth conditions.
item.dc:creator: Shun Muroga, Takashi Tsuji, Shunsuke Sakurai, Don N Futaba

item.title: Choosing a generator for streaming Gaussian noise in gravitational-wave mock data: accuracy, cost and reproducibility
item.description: arXiv:2611.01624v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mock data challenges need long stretches of colored Gaussian noise with a prescribed spectrum. The candidates are the crossfade of independently drawn windows that the standard gravitational-wave libraries implement, overlap-save finite-impulse-response filtering, autoregressive and autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) models, and the reproducible filter of PyCBC. One measure ranks them all: the covariance error against the target over the analysis band, evaluated from each generator's algebra; generated noise only checks the implementations. We also measure throughput, retained state and the cost of bit-exact regeneration. With the target continued smoothly below the band, the crossfade with windows of 256 s or more reaches an error below $10^{-3}$ on all eleven detector curves as tabulated, at about 4.7 million samples per second from a state of a few hundred bytes. An overlap-save filter is faster but needs tens of thousands of taps for an error of a few percent, and no tested autoregressive or ARMA configuration lies on the accuracy--throughput fronts. An error of $10^{-3}$ needs a window of 8 to 235 s, longest on the design curves with narrow lines, where it also depends on the tabulation. With the target cut at the band edge, as current generators do by default, every method has an error above one half on the projected Advanced LIGO (aLIGO) O4 curve, and the crossfade on five other curves. The crossfade is cyclostationary. With the continued target, its cyclic part is the larger part of the error only at 8 s, on the aLIGO O4 and the Virgo and KAGRA design curves, and stays within a factor of two of the stationary part on the aLIGO O3 and the Virgo and KAGRA design curves. We recommend the crossfade with a window from the table of detector curves, and a smooth continuation of the target below the band.
item.dc:creator: Isaac C. F. Wong

item.title: The Neural Density Model: An Open 3D Thermospheric Density Reanalysis for 2003--2026 From Tracked Space Debris
item.description: arXiv:2611.02103v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Thermospheric mass density controls satellite drag but is observed directly by few missions, and the leading operational product (HASDM) relies on non-public radar data. We present the Neural Density Model (NDM), a 3D density reanalysis for October 2003--October 2026 at 250--800~km. Previous approaches either convert the orbital decay of tracked objects into point densities or correct empirical models with a few global scale factors. NDM instead fits a spatially resolved neural correction to NRLMSISE-00 directly to the observed decay of 600--800 objects per year, through a differentiable drag operator, jointly with their ballistic coefficients, calibration spheres and accelerometer densities. On withheld satellites the median error is 0.078 (natural-log units), against 0.101 for HASDM and 0.310 for NRLMSISE-00; NDM has the smaller bias, HASDM slightly smaller scatter. On Spire GNSS orbits, never used in training, NDM and HASDM perform comparably. NDM uses only public observations.
item.dc:creator: Enrico Camporeale

item.title: Quantifying Bicycle Setup Differences on the Road: Field Estimates of CdA, Crr and Power Demand
item.description: arXiv:2611.03002v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Individual bicycle configurations can be assessed in situ using power and speed measurements without a velodrome or wind tunnel. We apply an integrated energy-balance workflow to five configurations tested by one rider on a road section. Five nominal power levels, each ridden in both directions, yield 25 paired observations. Kinetic-energy changes are corrected explicitly; gravitational work cancels between spatially matched outward and return sections. A shared effective rolling-resistance coefficient Crr and a separate aerodynamic drag area CdA for each setup are estimated jointly. The fitted drag areas range from 0.2288 to 0.3601m^2, with a common Crr=0.00551 +/- 0.00047. At 40km/h, the estimated differences are 17.4 +/- 5.5W favouring the EZ-covered over the uncovered 80mm rear-wheel configuration and 64.3 +/- 4.0W favouring the aerobar position over the drops on the tested road bike. The helmet swap yields a difference of 3.5 +/- 2.8W. Reported uncertainties combine statistical variability and assumed input uncertainties and represent one standard deviation. The study demonstrates a practical workflow for quantifying individual setup differences and connecting resistance estimates to power-speed predictions under specified reference conditions.
item.dc:creator: Mario Zin{\ss}er

item.title: Anomaly-ranked confirmation slows new-class learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.03250v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Anomaly detectors rank unfamiliar examples for expert confirmation, and the confirmed examples teach a classifier to recognise a new class. Across five benchmarks from physics, medicine and computer vision, the members flagged by the detector are those the classifier learns first. In three systems, confirming the highest-ranked members of a new class gives lower recognition than confirming the same number of random members. Handing subsequent selection to the promoted classifier recovers part of this loss in two systems. A paired intervention further shows that replacing nearby known classes with distant ones sharply reduces the confirmations needed for recognition. These results distinguish finding a new class from selecting examples that teach its extent: within the tested classes, concentrating confirmations at the top of the anomaly ranking makes learning less efficient.
item.dc:creator: Argyro Sasli, Michael Coughlin

item.title: A Probability Model for Pentagonal Prism Dice Rolls
item.description: arXiv:2609.01643v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the realm of probability theory and game design, the study of dice probabilities plays a crucial role. The featured dice are usually fair, so their probabilities can be predicted without rolling the dice. Pentagonal prismatic dice are not fair. Hence, the probabilities are more complicated. Our mathematical model is naturally derived from both the geometric properties of the dice and empirical evidence. Dice of varying sizes but with constant volume were designed. Using a 3D printer with 100 percent infill, the dice were printed and prepared. A machine that simulates dropping dice through a dice tower onto a hard surface was used to obtain about 41,000 results. From these data, a statistical model was constructed that gives probabilities of dice with varying height-to-radius ratios. The formula for the model is based on the centroid solid angle, but with two adjustment parameters due to varying energy and other requirements to transition between different resting aspects. Within the range of height-to-radius ratios tested, the data are within reasonable statistical error of the model.
item.dc:creator: Paul R. Hurst, J. Naleo Hyde

item.title: Annealing chains that communicate: low-energy cluster structures across engines with one configuration
item.description: arXiv:2302.02811v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The global minimum of a cluster decides which structure a simulation predicts. We present anneal, a global optimizer of communicating chains. Each chain draws its move by Thompson sampling from a Normal-Gamma posterior on quench depth. A stalled chain completes the orbits of a symmetric core. A chain retires on a Good-Turing estimate of its unseen mass, a rule with a Lean derivation. The chains share minima through an annealed-flow bank, and a ledger charges each force call to the chain that spent it. On 64 shared starts of LJ$_{38}$ and LJ$_{75}$ the hop matches the hit rate of GMIN, 64 of 64, at a lower median cost a paired test does not separate. On the Cambridge Morse table it reaches 145 of 244 targets and GMIN 131.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Goswami, Ruhila Goswami, Amrita Goswami, Moritz Sallermann, Sonaly Goswami, Debabrata Goswami

item.title: Bayesian phase transition for the critical Ising model: Enlarged replica symmetry in the epsilon expansion and in 2D
item.description: arXiv:2604.23346v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A process that images or measures bond energies in the critical Ising model can be in distinct measurement 'phases', depending on the precision of measurement. We study the transition into the strong-measurement phase using replica field theory (an epsilon expansion around six dimensions), a symmetry analysis, and numerical simulations in two dimensions. The results show that certain inference problems possess unexpected structure associated with an enlarged symmetry of the replica description. The symmetry imposes constraints on correlation functions, and is an analog of the Nishimori phenomenon in the Ising spin glass, but in a distinct replica limit. It determines the exact critical exponent for an Edwards-Anderson-like correlator in the measured Ising model, both in 2D and near the upper critical dimension. The symmetry is present microscopically for certain measurement protocols, and it emerges in the infrared for generic protocols at the critical measurement strength. We also examine the epsilon expansion for models with power-law interactions and/or long-range measurement. Finally, we describe an analogous replica symmetry enlargement for measurement in Wegner's lattice gauge theory.
item.dc:creator: Kay Joerg Wiese, Alapan Das, Adam Nahum

item.title: Virtual-Array Operational Modal Analysis of Rolling Tires Using a Single Tire Cavity Accelerometer
item.description: arXiv:2606.10437v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The dynamics of the rolling tire govern structure-borne road noise below 500 Hz. Laser Doppler vibrometry (LDV) is the established laboratory reference for measuring rolling-tire modes. This paper presents a complementary approach that uses a single wireless tire cavity accelerometer (TCA) mounted on the inner liner and a once-per-revolution encoder on the drum of a tire-on-drum rig fitted with a cleat. Because the drum-to-tire diameter ratio (2.74) is non-integer, successive cleat impacts encounter the TCA at different circumferential positions. The TCA's contact-patch signature locates the sensor at each impact within approximately $1^\circ$, and grouping the impact responses by angular position synthesizes a 36-element virtual array from a single 128 s run. Covariance-driven stochastic subspace identification (SSI-COV) is applied using a consensus rule across multiple parameter settings, bootstrap resampling over impacts, and a correction for window-induced damping; the complete signal-processing chain is verified on synthetic data with known modes. For a slick 195/65R15 tire rolling at 30 km/h under a 1334 N load, ten modes between 46 and 193 Hz are robustly identified, exhibiting circumferential wavenumbers from 1 to 5, damping ratios of 2.1--4.2%, and strongly complex mode shapes, with three additional modes identified tentatively. The extracted modes follow the wavenumber ladder of a stationary modal test of the same tire. Requiring no optical access and capturing the full virtual array in a single run, the proposed method is well suited to treaded tires and on-road testing, at the expense of in-tire sensor installation.
item.dc:creator: Pradosh Pritam Dash, Pablo A Tarazaga

item.title: Learning by Confusion Locates a Parametrization-Dependent Fisher Information Maximum
item.description: arXiv:2610.34769v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning by confusion (LBC) is a machine-learning method for locating phase transitions without assuming a known order parameter. Its characteristic accuracy curve contains a central maximum that is interpreted as the transition point, but what determines the location and finite-size scaling of this maximum has remained unclear. We derive an exact balance condition for the Bayes-optimal confusion peak and show that, for equilibrium systems with a single swept parameter, the peak closely follows the maximum of the corresponding Fisher information. This immediately gives its finite-size scaling and reveals an unexpected dependence on how the data are sampled: the same configurations arranged on grids uniform in $T$, $\ln T$, or $\beta=1/T$ can yield different finite-size pseudocritical trajectories. Tests on the Ising, Blume-Capel, Potts, and Baxter-Wu models confirm the prediction across continuous, tricritical, and first-order transitions. Our results identify the statistical quantity measured by LBC and show that finite-size machine-learning estimates can depend on the parametrization of the training data as well as on the underlying physics.
item.dc:creator: George Issa, Richard Scalettar
